Pit River Tribe

Also find this entry through: Pit River Tribe (Ajumawi–Atsugewi Nation)

The Pit River Tribe is a living collective government of eleven autonomous bands in northeastern California. This starting guide distinguishes the government, individual band routes and broader Achumawi and Atsugewi reading labels. Its selected sources connect band authority with contemporary language, environmental and community work; the collection remains unfinished.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Eleven bands within a collective government

The Tribe’s published constitution names Ajumawi, Atsugewi, Atwamsini, Ilmawi, Astarawi, Hammawi, Hewisedawi, Itsatawi, Aporige, Kosalektawi and Madesi. Its posted text recalls the 1964 constitution and is marked updated July 2005. It provides collective representation while recognizing band cultural responsibilities. The eleven band routes below make those names separately findable; they do not imply eleven separately verified federal recognitions or identical community histories.

Read the sources [1] Pit River Tribe

02

Environmental responsibilities and community learning

The Environmental Programs Office describes water monitoring, ecological restoration, youth science education, gardens and a native-plant greenhouse among its responsibilities. The Tribe’s November 2025 newsletter reports greenhouse renewal and a language camp held at Lassen on August 30. These are collective institutional descriptions and dated event reports. They do not assign every activity or participant to one band, establish present fluency, or demonstrate completed ecological outcomes.

Read the sources [2] Pit River Tribe [3] Pit River Tribe

03

Band histories need their own evidence

Shared government does not make one band’s account interchangeable with another’s. The constitutional text recognizes individual band responsibilities for cultural matters. This directory therefore links specific band routes with visible identification references and records remaining source and image gaps. The historical photograph shown here is a Hat Creek Atsugewi example; it is not a portrait of the tribal government or a visual substitute for all eleven bands.

Read the sources [1] Pit River Tribe

04

Four Corners in a dated congressional account

A September 2026 Senate committee report places the proposed Four Corners transfer within a longer history of Pit River land loss and political organizing. It connects the 1970 occupation near Burney with the Tribe’s later effort to acquire that property. The report draws on testimony and published history; those underlying works require their own review. This is a collective Pit River account, rather than an Atsugewi-only chronology or a court determination of present land title.

Read the sources [4] United States Senate Committee on Indian Affairs / U.S. Government Publishing Office

05

Following a legislative step without assuming the outcome

The committee report recommends an amended bill. A separate Senate text dated September 30, 2026 records passage with an amendment and sets out transfer, trust and survey provisions for Four Corners. Reading the two documents together distinguishes a legislative proposal from its historical justification. This dated bill version alone does not establish later enactment, a completed conveyance or present ownership; those questions need later official records.

Read the sources [4] United States Senate Committee on Indian Affairs / U.S. Government Publishing Office [5] United States Congress / U.S. Government Publishing Office

Constitution of the Pit River Tribe ↗

Publication: 1964 adoption; published text updated July 2005

Read the preamble and Articles I–II, VI and VII, including band powers. The Tribe publishes this text as adopted in 1964 and updated July 2005. It distinguishes the eleven-band political entity from language labels and recognizes band cultural authority. No complete 2026 legal consolidation, title survey or independent jurisdictional ruling is inferred.

Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026 — Senate Report 119-147 ↗

Publication: 2026-09-22

A dated committee account connects the proposed Four Corners transfer with earlier land loss and the 1970 occupation. Its historical synthesis cites testimony and scholarship, which are not thereby independently inspected. Read it as collective Pit River legislative context, not an Atsugewi-only chronology or a court finding.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual GovInfo HTML header/date, Purpose, selected Background and Need paragraphs, Summary and Legislative History: primary web-reader lines0–160. Particular close reading of land-loss discussion80–93 and Four Corners account113–132. Later executive testimony and the underlying cited books/hearings were not closely reviewed.

Review recorded: October 31, 2026

Access note: Exact normal terminal HTML retrieval returned200 and was saved privately. Report recommendation and proposed provisions do not establish current enactment, completed trust transfer, land ownership or programme outcomes. Current legislative status was not inspected in this bounded source packet; no present non-enactment claim is made. The report's rancheria/acreage/participant/arrest totals and its place-specific legal characterizations are not adopted.
